commits.subject: Catch the wrong-language failure by reading the transcript, not the metadata
commits.body:
The guard written for Lab v0's worst failure could not see it. On 2026-08-21
Sarvam returned fluent romanized ARABIC for an English engineering lecture and
reported `language_code: "en-IN"` -- the same code the run was configured with.
`buildProvenance` compares exactly those two fields, so on the one run it was
written for, it stayed silent. The only thing that flagged that transcript was
the engine's own 0.617 confidence clearing the 0.8 threshold by 0.183. At 0.85
the same Arabic text would have carried no warning at all.

Found by driving all three captured fixtures through the running server rather
than by reading the code, which is the only way it could have been found: the
branch is unreachable for every response in the repo.

`checkTranscriptLanguage()` reads the text instead. Function-word density is
crude on purpose -- the separation is an order of magnitude, measured over the
three real responses:

  real English (en-IN, p=0.846)      42.5% English function words
  romanized Arabic (en-IN, p=0.617)   3.9%
  Devanagari Hindi (hi-IN, p=0.999)  76.3% Devanagari characters

It appends a limitation and never blocks or edits a transcript, refuses to
judge anything under 120 tokens, and says nothing for `unknown` (auto-detect
already carries its own limitation). Verified end to end: the misdetected
lecture's stored provenance now reads "The transcript does not read as English:
only 4.3% of its words are common English function words."

Also: `language_probability` gets a structured home on ProcessingProvenance.
It survived only as prose inside `limitations`, so "show me every lecture
transcribed below 0.8" -- the exact sweep that would surface this class of
failure -- was not a query anyone could write.

Plus two things the verification needed and found missing: `scripts/setup-storage.mts`,
which package.json referenced and which did not exist (it lists buckets rather
than probing, because a missing bucket comes back as status 400 with statusCode
"404" as a *string* in a different field, which is what broke Lab v0's version);
and `scripts/verify-languages.mts`, which drives the Hindi and misdetected
fixtures end to end -- 33 checks, and it pins median segment duration at 17.4s
so the chunk-grouping regression cannot come back unnoticed.

New suite scripts/test-provenance.mts: 16 checks against the real fixtures.

Also records the 2026-08-22 decision in .knowledge/decisions.md. Building the
Product Platform crosses the frozen walkthrough protocol's stopping rule
completely -- `extraction_candidates.kind` encodes the domain model in a check
constraint before the walkthrough that was meant to validate it. That was
flagged before work began and needed to be written down, with its cost stated,
rather than left in a chat log.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.subject: ClassMind V1: verify the end-to-end workflow, and fix what verifying it exposed
commits.body:
The product platform built up to this point had never been driven. Lint, tsc
and build all passed, which says nothing about whether a faculty member can get
from an upload to a student reading a confirmed deadline. Two things were
needed to find out, and running it found a real defect.

**A fixture transcription provider** (`src/lib/transcription/fixture.ts`),
selected by `TRANSCRIPTION_PROVIDER=fixture`. It replays three verbatim Sarvam
Batch responses captured during Lab v0 RUN 1 and exported once to
`fixtures/transcription/` -- the product never reads Lab v0's `runs` table. The
response bytes are real, so normalization, evidence offsets and provenance are
all exercised against a genuine transcript rather than against a synthesised
one; only the network call and the queue delay are simulated. Sarvam stays the
default so nothing can fall back to replay by accident, and every provenance
record written this way says REPLAYED, NOT TRANSCRIBED in its limitations.

**An end-to-end driver** (`scripts/e2e.mts`) that drives the running server over
HTTP exactly as a browser does: sign in, create a course, add context, upload
10.5 MB of real audio through the signed URL, transcribe, poll, extract,
confirm/edit/reject, then re-enter as a student and ask a question. 67 checks,
0 failures. The load-bearing ones are negative: a student's lecture payload
carries zero candidates, a student cannot rule on one or trigger extraction,
and the anon key cannot read any of the four tables directly.

**The defect it exposed.** The rules engine read an 18-minute university
course-outline lecture as 2 generic guidance items. It missed the entire
module-by-module syllabus and the prescribed textbook -- the only two things in
that lecture a student actually needs. The lexicon was built from a Class-12
coaching lecture, so it knew "homework", "DPP" and "notes on Telegram" and had
no rule for a lecturer walking through a syllabus.

Fixed by adding two rules, both at suppression "none" because every sentence
they exist to catch is first-person-plural and veto A would delete all of them:

  exam_scope.course_coverage      gated on a curricular unit noun, so
                                  "we will look at the compressor" stays silent
                                  while "in the second module we discuss..."
                                  fires
  announcement.prescribed_material  a named textbook plus a prescription cue,
                                  so "buy this" is separated from "a book exists"

Same lecture now yields 21 candidates. Method version bumped 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0:
a stored candidate names the version that produced it, and two rule sets
sharing one version string would make every earlier accuracy number unreadable.

Extraction suite 65 -> 75 cases, including the negative gates.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
